newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK PRESIDENT MAY RUN AGAIN IF ASKED-SPOKESMAN.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK PRESIDENT MAY RUN AGAIN IF ASKED-SPOKESMAN.

text.p: Slovak President Michal Kovac would consider standing for a second term next year if asked by top political forces, his spokesman said on Tuesday.

"The president himself decided to not stand in the next presidential elections," the spokesman, Vladimir Stefko, told Reuters. "But he could revise this decision if asked to stand by significant political powers or parties."
On Friday and Saturday, Slovakia will hold a referendum on whether the president should be elected directly instead of by a weighted majority in parliament as is currently the case.
The vote will take place alongside another referendum on whether Slovakia should join NATO. The common date for both referendums was set by Kovac.

The political referendum is seen as an attempt to prevent the controversial prime minister, Vladimir Meciar, from possibly assuming presidential powers when the term of Kovac, an avowed foe of Meciar, ends next March.
On Tuesday the independent daily Sme quoted Kovac as saying he would quit politics and not stand for president again.
"The President said this to show that a direct presidential election was not a mere tool to ensure his further existence at the post," Stefko said.
"But this does not mean he would definitely reject a possible nomination by significant political forces."
The referendum on direct presidential elections resulted from a petition drive led by opposition parties. Kovac and the parliamentary opposition have urged Slovaks to vote "yes" in both referendums.

Meciar and allies in his three-party cabinet have strongly opposed the presidential referendum, saying it would illegaly change the constitution. Last week the Slovak Constitutional Court rejected a government motion to declare it illegal.

Meciar said Kovac supported direct presidential elections because he aimed to run again but knew that neither the ruling coalition nor the opposition would be able to muster the two-thirds majority to push their nominee through.
